scenario: AITA for not wanting to attend my great aunt's funeral? | So today I came home from college (Britain, so American High School, I think). The second I walk through the door my mum tells me that her grandma's sister has died. "Your great aunt Wyn died and the funeral will probably be soon." My first thoughts were 'Who?' and 'Why is she telling me this?' I have actually never heard this name before or met this person besides the one time I found out today I had met her when I was still extremely young and unable to walk for myself. This turned into a slight argument as, for some reason, she wanted me to go this funeral, despite knowing I am a really awkward person at funeral's for people I've met more than once, let along a funeral for someone I've met only once and have no idea who is part of the family. The argument ends with her trying to guilt-trip me by outright just saying "Fine, I'll go on my own." in a really sulky way. Her only arguments for me going were that I'd be going out of 'respect' and support for her, despite that she has never once mentioned this great aunt to me even though she supposedly played a massive hand in raising her as my grandmother, and that it's one of the few times we'll see the much larger branch of the family where it's likely to be a few hundred of us, about 10 of which I have seen more than once but still at most 10 times, maybe not even that. To me, it would feel like gatecrashing the funeral for someone else's family and that, even though I am part of the family, no one would want me there since I do not know nor did I know the person who died. I don't know how much this takes precedence over everything else but it felt like it had to reiterated a lot - I have never met this person besides the one time she met me when I was either 1 or 2 years old and the name has never been mentioned to me before now, at least not to my recollection. So, AITA for not wanting to attend someone who is practically a stranger to me's wedding for the sole reason that she's family?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for the person in this scenario not to attend their great aunt's funeral. Let me break this down step by step.

First, the person just came home from college in Britain, which is like high school in America. Their mom tells them that their great aunt Wyn has died. The person's initial reaction is confusion because they've never heard of this great aunt before and only met her once when they were very young, like 1 or 2 years old. They don't remember meeting her, and the name hasn't been mentioned before.

The mom wants the person to attend the funeral, but the person feels awkward at funerals, especially for people they don't know well. They argue, and the mom guilt-trips them by saying she'll go alone. The mom's reasons are respect and support, but she's never mentioned the great aunt before, even though she supposedly played a big role in raising her. The person feels like gatecrashing a family event because they don't know the person who died and only know a few family members.

The person is asking if they're AITA (Ask if I'm the Asshole) for not wanting to go to the funeral because the great aunt is practically a stranger, even though she's family.

So, is it morally acceptable for the person not to attend the funeral?

I think about the reasons for attending a funeral. Usually, it's to show respect for the deceased and support for the grieving family. But in this case, the person has no personal connection to the great aunt. They've only met her once when they were a baby and don't remember her. The mom has never mentioned her before, so the person feels disconnected.

The person feels like they don't know the family well enough to attend the funeral. They might feel out of place and uncomfortable, which is a valid feeling. It's not about being disrespectful but about their own comfort and ability to contribute positively to the event.

On the other hand, the mom is insisting they go, citing respect and family support. But if the person doesn't feel connected, forcing them to attend might not be helpful. It could make the situation more stressful for everyone.

I also consider cultural and familial expectations. In some cultures, attending family funerals is a strong tradition, and not attending could be seen as disrespectful. But in this case, the person's mom hasn't emphasized the great aunt's importance before, so it's confusing why she's pushing now.

The person's feelings of being a stranger at the funeral are valid. They might not know how to behave or interact with extended family they don't know well. It's important to respect their boundaries and feelings.

In conclusion, while attending a funeral is often seen as a respectful action, it's also important to consider the individual's feelings and connection to the deceased. If the person feels no personal connection and attending would cause them distress, it might be morally acceptable for them not to attend.
